prompt: What is the write latency at W = 2, and how many replica failures can writes survive?
scenario: A key has N = 3 replicas. They acknowledge writes in 3 ms, 9 ms and 60 ms.

options.text: 60 ms; writes survive one replica failure
9 ms; writes survive one replica failure
3 ms; writes survive two replica failures
24 ms (the mean); writes survive no failures

explanation: The coordinator returns after the second-fastest ack, 9 ms, and writes keep succeeding with N − W = 1 replica down. 60 ms would be W = 3, which survives no failures. 3 ms and two failures describe W = 1. Quorum latency is an order statistic, not an average.

prompt: Each of three replicas is independently up 99% of the time. Roughly how available are writes at W = 3?

options.text: About 99.97%, better than a single replica
About 99%, the same as a single replica
About 97%, worse than a single replica
About 99.9999%, since there are three copies

explanation: W = 3 needs all three up: 0.99³ ≈ 0.9703. 99.97% is the W = 2 figure (at least 2 of 3 up). Equal to a single replica ignores that any of three can fail. 99.9999% is W = 1 (at least one up). Requiring every replica multiplies their failure chances.

prompt: How many replicas must respond, and does a write in DC1 at this level guarantee a read in DC2 at the same level sees it?
scenario: A Cassandra keyspace has replication factor 3 in each of two data centres, DC1 and DC2. The team is choosing between QUORUM and LOCAL_QUORUM.

options.text: QUORUM: 4 of 6 replicas, and yes, since 4 + 4 > 6
QUORUM: 2 per DC, and yes, since each DC overlaps
LOCAL_QUORUM: 4 of 6, and no, the DCs never sync
LOCAL_QUORUM: 2 local, and yes, since 2 + 2 > 3

explanation: QUORUM is ⌊(3 + 3) ÷ 2⌋ + 1 = 4 of all 6 replicas, and 4 + 4 > 6 guarantees overlap across data centres. Two per DC is EACH_QUORUM's rule, not QUORUM's. LOCAL_QUORUM is 2 in the local DC; the DCs do replicate, but asynchronously. A DC1 write and a DC2 read at LOCAL_QUORUM touch disjoint replicas, so 2 + 2 > 3 is the wrong comparison and there is no guarantee.

prompt: Why does R + W > N guarantee that a read contacts a replica holding the latest successful write?

options.text: The coordinator always forwards reads to the replica that took the write
Disjoint read and write sets would need more distinct replicas than exist
Replicas synchronise before each read, so all of them are up to date
A majority of replicas always agree on a value, so reads see that value

explanation: If a read set of R and a write set of W were disjoint, the cluster would need R + W distinct replicas, more than N, so they must share one. Coordinators don't track which replica took the write. Replicas don't synchronise before reads. R and W need not be majorities, and replicas can disagree; the read picks the newest version it sees.

prompt: What best explains what the three clients saw?
scenario: N = 3, W = 2, R = 2, with read repair done asynchronously. Client 1 writes seat = Maya; only replica A acks before the timeout, so client 1 is told the write failed. Client 2 then reads from A and B and sees Maya. Client 3 reads from B and C and sees the seat free.

options.text: A bug, since R + W > N rules out any stale reads
Expected: failed writes are kept, not rolled back
A sign that client clocks were skewed by a lot
A sloppy quorum must have accepted the write

explanation: A write that reaches fewer than W replicas is reported as failed but isn't rolled back, so A keeps Maya and some reads see it while later ones don't: non-linearizable despite R + W > N. The overlap rule only covers successful writes, so this is not a bug. No timestamps conflict here, so skew isn't involved. A sloppy quorum would have counted a stand-in and reported success.

prompt: Which can make a store with R + W > N return results that are not linearizable? Select all that apply.

options.text: Two concurrent writes resolved by last-write-wins
Writes counted on stand-in nodes in a sloppy quorum
Choosing W = 3 and R = 1 with N = 3 for the key
A replica rebuilt from a copy holding an old value

explanation: Last-write-wins can drop one of two concurrent writes; sloppy quorums count acks outside the home replicas, so reads may miss them; and restoring a replica from a stale copy can leave fewer than W replicas holding the write. W = 3, R = 1 is a valid strict-quorum setting (4 > 3) and is not itself a cause.

prompt: Why did the read return the old value?
scenario: Home replicas B and C for key K are partitioned from the coordinator. A write of K = v2 is acknowledged by home replica A and by stand-in node D, so W = 2 is met. Moments later a read with R = 2 reaches B and C and returns v1.

options.text: R was set too low, since R = 3 always returns v2 here
The write used a sloppy quorum, so overlap was lost
B and C had a clock skew problem with their timestamps
Read repair overwrote v2 on node A with the older v1

explanation: D's ack counted toward W but D is not a home replica, so the write and read sets (A, D) and (B, C) don't overlap until hinted handoff delivers v2 to B. R = 3 would have caught A, but B and C could still be the only reachable home replicas, so 'always' is wrong. Clock skew doesn't matter: B and C never received v2. Read repair propagates the newest version, so it wouldn't overwrite v2 with v1.

prompt: In Cassandra, which statement about hints is correct?

options.text: Hints count toward every consistency level, which is how sloppy quorums work
Hints are kept indefinitely, so repair is unnecessary after an outage
Hints only count toward ANY; down past the hint window, a node needs repair
Hints are kept by the client driver and replayed when its connection resumes

explanation: Cassandra's coordinator stores hints for unreachable replicas; they satisfy only consistency level ANY, and are not kept for a node down longer than max_hint_window (3 hours by default), after which repair is needed. They don't count toward other levels, aren't kept forever, and live on the coordinator node, not in the client driver.

prompt: Why is read repair not enough on its own to keep replicas consistent?

options.text: It only runs at consistency level ALL
It only repairs keys that are being read
It copies the oldest version, not newest
It can only repair replicas in one rack

explanation: Read repair is triggered by reads, so cold keys stay stale indefinitely; anti-entropy covers them. It runs at levels above ONE, not only ALL. It writes the newest version to stale replicas, not the oldest. It has no rack restriction.

prompt: About how much data must the replicas exchange to find the difference?
scenario: Two replicas each hold 1,000,000 keys and differ in exactly one key. They use Merkle trees with 65,536 leaves (16 levels) and 16-byte hashes.

options.text: 16 MB: one hash for each of the keys
1 MB: one hash for each of the leaves
16 bytes: a single root hash compared
About 512 bytes of hashes, then ~15 keys

explanation: The replicas descend one path: two child hashes at each of 16 levels is 32 × 16 bytes = 512 bytes, then exchange the ~15 keys in the differing leaf. 16 MB is the no-tree approach. Sending every leaf hash (65,536 × 16 bytes ≈ 1 MB) ignores the tree's structure. A single root hash only tells them a difference exists, not where.

prompt: What is the most likely cause?
scenario: A Cassandra cluster uses the default gc_grace_seconds. A node was down for two days last month and was brought back without running repair. Rows deleted during that outage have started reappearing in reads this week.

options.text: Tombstones were purged before the node got them; it resurrected the rows
The deletes ran at consistency level ONE, so they were never persisted
Hinted handoff replayed the original inserts after the deletes were done
Read repair always prefers live data over tombstones when it merges rows

explanation: The returning node missed the tombstones (its outage exceeded the 3-hour hint window) and, without repair, still held the rows. After 10 days the other replicas purged their tombstones, so repair or read repair now copies the old rows back. A delete at ONE is still persisted on one replica. Hinted handoff delivers writes in their original order with timestamps, so it can't undo a later delete. Read repair resolves by timestamp; a newer tombstone wins over older data.
